texts.orig: (TBI) during a Muay Thai sparring session in San Francisco. I immediately suspected something was wrong as I felt a strange sensation in my head, but as I had no other symptoms, I didn’t think too much of it and kept going on with my life as normal.
texts.text: (TBI) during a Muay Thai sparring session in San Francisco. I immediately suspected something was wrong as I felt a strange sensation in my head, but as I had no other symptoms, I didn’t think too much of it and kept going on with my life as normal.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Two weeks later, I suddenly felt extremely dizzy and started to get painful headaches. I knew I was in big trouble when I tried to read a book but couldn’t understand what the sentences meant. Individual words were fine, but when I tried to string together a whole sentence, it just wouldn’t click. My symptoms began to spiral, and before I knew it I found myself in the emergency room.
texts.text: Two weeks later, I suddenly felt extremely dizzy and started to get painful headaches. I knew I was in big trouble when I tried to read a book but couldn’t understand what the sentences meant. Individual words were fine, but when I tried to string together a whole sentence, it just wouldn’t click. My symptoms began to spiral, and before I knew it I found myself in the emergency room.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: What I thought would be a quick stint on the sidelines turned into the most difficult and prolonged ordeal of my life. I was on disability leave for nearly a year, and even today I’m still not fully recovered. It’s been a tough experience, but one that in a strange way I’m immensely grateful for. What I’ve learned from the process, which I’ll be sharing in today’s post, has been a huge unlock both as a PM and in life more broadly.

I was generally unable to take care of myself, and without the support of my amazing partner, I’m really not sure how I would have gotten by.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Reorienting my life to compensate for my injury has left me with some invaluable knowledge across both my personal and professional life. In this post, I’m going to share a range of frameworks and actionable tips that’ll help you better manage your energy and emotions as a PM, while becoming a happier human being in general.
texts.text: Reorienting my life to compensate for my injury has left me with some invaluable knowledge across both my personal and professional life. In this post, I’m going to share a range of frameworks and actionable tips that’ll help you better manage your energy and emotions as a PM, while becoming a happier human being in general.

This led to a range of issues, including excessive anxiety, insomnia, digestive issues, higher cortisol, and more.

texts.orig: So. . . what can you do about this? The answer lies in stimulating the parasympathetic rest-and-digest system. This response reduces baseline levels of stress and is also a useful tool to remain calm in high-stakes situations—such as a contentious product review. A decent chunk of my recovery journey and what I cover below ties back to this core, overarching principle.

texts.orig: In my case, the TBI meant that in my first few months back at work, I simply didn’t have the physical tolerance that I had in the past. I needed to take breaks, I couldn’t work long hours, and I had to prioritize my health and recovery over anything else (yes, that included my OKRs!).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: One of the most helpful changes I made was to set a limit of how much I would work in a day. I restricted myself to working around two hours less per day than my pre-injury baseline. I took additional breaks during the day and avoided working late into the evening.

texts.orig: In TBI recovery, excessive anxious and depressive feelings kick off a self-reinforcing negative loop that impedes recovery. Higher stress leads to sympathetic dominance of the nervous system as the fight-or-flight response gets stuck in overdrive. Sympathetic dominance causes insomnia, which has a huge impact, given how critical sleep is for TBI recovery. Sympathetic dominance also causes digestive issues such as irritable bowel syndrome and nausea, both of which in turn lead to more anxiety and stress.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: My primary fear was that I’d never be able to return to work. While my doctors were unclear on how long my recovery would take, they did believe that there was a decent chance I’d eventually recover enough to get back to a job. Nonetheless, I played out the scenario of never being able to work again. I had long-term disability coverage and was lucky enough to have a very supportive partner who could help take care of me. I reasoned that in the worst case, I could move to my native country, Australia, and at least have health-care coverage and some degree of welfare support. I knew that while not being able to work would be a very painful future, I would find a way to survive if it did end up happening.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In the case of alcohol, many TBI patients experience a spike in symptoms after having as little as one or two drinks. Alcohol also affects sleep, causes inflammation, and increases the chances of re-injury due to impaired coordination.

texts.orig: It’s now been over a year and a half since I last drank alcohol or caffeinated beverages, and I couldn’t be happier with my decision.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Since giving up alcohol, I’ve absolutely loved getting up early on weekends and being hangover-free. I feel better and have more energy throughout the day, and also save a lot of money. Socializing while sober was tough at the start, but I’ve gotten used to it over time. Today, I’m generally very much at ease in social settings despite being fully sober. The increasing popularity of non-alcoholic beer and cocktails with 0.0% ABV makes it even easier.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Caffeine has been slightly harder. Getting back to work was a tough jolt to the system, and the fatigue I was running into definitely made me miss drinking caffeine. Having said that, my energy has improved over time, and I can now work at a high-output level without needing any caffeine. I do miss a good matcha latte, though. 😢

texts.orig: Beyond managing my energy and emotions, I’ve also realized how important of a role perspective plays. Being intentional with perspective-taking improves life satisfaction, while making it easier to undertake desired life changes.
texts.text: Beyond managing my energy and emotions, I’ve also realized how important of a role perspective plays. Being intentional with perspective-taking improves life satisfaction, while making it easier to undertake desired life changes.

texts.orig: Taking on something positive that you enjoy
texts.text: Taking on something positive that you enjoy

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The first few months after my accident were the toughest. I couldn’t play sports, work, listen to music, watch Netflix, travel, hang out with friends, and so on. It felt like I’d lost all the joy in my life, as I could no longer do most of the activities that I ordinarily loved.
texts.text: The first few months after my accident were the toughest. I couldn’t play sports, work, listen to music, watch Netflix, travel, hang out with friends, and so on. It felt like I’d lost all the joy in my life, as I could no longer do most of the activities that I ordinarily loved.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: My lesson here is that when life goes south, you need to find at least one activity that brings positivity to your life. Having just one positive thing to look forward to can flip your perspective on life, even if everything else is completely fucked.

texts.orig: Meditation
texts.text: Meditation

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Initially when I couldn’t do anything else, meditation was my savior. I’d been meditating on and off for a decade and had always wanted to go much deeper into the practice. In this sense, my injury was a blessing, as I had months on end where I couldn’t do much else. It just so happened that meditation was also beneficial to my recovery.
texts.text: Initially when I couldn’t do anything else, meditation was my savior. I’d been meditating on and off for a decade and had always wanted to go much deeper into the practice. In this sense, my injury was a blessing, as I had months on end where I couldn’t do much else. It just so happened that meditation was also beneficial to my recovery.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: For the longest time, I’d wanted to do a meditation retreat but couldn’t find the time to prioritize it. After my injury, I had nothing but time. A few months into my recovery, I mustered up the courage to go on my first seven-day silent Vipassana retreat at Spirit Rock, a well-known meditation center in Northern California. I had such a blast that I went on another silent retreat at Spirit Rock just two months after my first!

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Because I was finally able to go deeper on meditation, the feeling of months going by where I did “nothing” no longer felt like wasted time. Instead, it began to feel like a unique opportunity to pursue a lifelong passion.

texts.orig: Writing
texts.text: Writing

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Another long-term unfulfilled desire had been to start writing online in some capacity. I’d just never found the time or the right moment to get started.
texts.text: Another long-term unfulfilled desire had been to start writing online in some capacity. I’d just never found the time or the right moment to get started.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As I slowly increased my screen time tolerance, my doctor told me to take on more cognitively challenging tasks to prepare myself for eventually going back to a full-time job. After initial hesitation, I started writing about my injury and recovery on a blog. As my recovery progressed and I started to think about returning to work, I switched over to writing about recent product and experiment launches.

texts.orig: Taking a wider perspective
texts.text: Taking a wider perspective

texts.label: text
texts.orig: They say that success rarely looks linear, and instead more closely resembles a squiggly chaotic line that goes all over the place before eventually heading up and to the right (in the ideal world).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: My recovery process was a squiggly line in every regard. So many times, just when things were starting to get better, I’d have a major setback and feel like I lost months of progress. To say this was demoralizing would be the understatement of the year.
texts.text: My recovery process was a squiggly line in every regard. So many times, just when things were starting to get better, I’d have a major setback and feel like I lost months of progress. To say this was demoralizing would be the understatement of the year.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In these moments, it was very difficult to not lose hope, as the “I’m never going to get better” narrative would take hold. During one of these setbacks, my therapist asked me an important question.
texts.text: In these moments, it was very difficult to not lose hope, as the “I’m never going to get better” narrative would take hold. During one of these setbacks, my therapist asked me an important question.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “How wide is your frame of reference?”
texts.text: “How wide is your frame of reference?”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: When suffering from strong and painful symptoms, I often defaulted to a very narrow view of my recovery. What I would miss was that even if the preceding days or weeks had not been great, if I zoomed out to take a wider frame of reference, it was clear that the overall trend line was positive.
texts.text: When suffering from strong and painful symptoms, I often defaulted to a very narrow view of my recovery. What I would miss was that even if the preceding days or weeks had not been great, if I zoomed out to take a wider frame of reference, it was clear that the overall trend line was positive.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Learning to take a wider frame was extremely helpful when the going got tough, and this principle has strong applicability in a broader life context.
texts.text: Learning to take a wider frame was extremely helpful when the going got tough, and this principle has strong applicability in a broader life context.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Let’s say you’ve been hard at work on a project or improving some aspect of yourself. If the goal is lofty enough, you’ll inevitably run into major obstacles. You’ll feel like you’re hitting a wall and question whether you’ll ever reach your goal.
texts.text: Let’s say you’ve been hard at work on a project or improving some aspect of yourself. If the goal is lofty enough, you’ll inevitably run into major obstacles. You’ll feel like you’re hitting a wall and question whether you’ll ever reach your goal.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Zooming out and taking a wider frame of reference is helpful in a bi-directional way. Looking at progress over months and years instead of days and weeks may help you realize that in fact you are progressing, and that it makes sense to stay the course.

texts.text: A new lease on life

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It’s been a tough ride, to say the least, but I’m immensely grateful for my TBI journey. There was no escaping my situation, and being forced to face my challenges head-on has left me with knowledge that has significantly improved the quality of my personal and professional life.
texts.text: It’s been a tough ride, to say the least, but I’m immensely grateful for my TBI journey. There was no escaping my situation, and being forced to face my challenges head-on has left me with knowledge that has significantly improved the quality of my personal and professional life.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: I’m thankfully continuing to get better and better over time. Last month I went scuba diving in the Great Barrier Reef, and in December I’m flying to Nepal to do Everest Base Camp. In true growth PM fashion, I also successfully converted my girlfriend to fiancée!

texts.orig: All of us will experience a major decline in health at some point. That’s life, until the day we’re no longer here. However, we can maximize the probability of staying healthy over the long run by maintaining positive habits and lifestyle choices.
texts.text: All of us will experience a major decline in health at some point. That’s life, until the day we’re no longer here. However, we can maximize the probability of staying healthy over the long run by maintaining positive habits and lifestyle choices.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Working hard is undoubtedly important, but it’s also critical to do whatever you can to reduce the physical and emotional load caused by an ambitious career.
texts.text: Working hard is undoubtedly important, but it’s also critical to do whatever you can to reduce the physical and emotional load caused by an ambitious career.

texts.orig: I consider myself fortunate to have experienced firsthand what it’s like to be disabled for an extended period of time, and I now have a much deeper appreciation of just how awesome life is when you have great health. Do not take it for granted.
